title: Window Replacement in Roseburg, Oregon
excerpt: Window replacement in Roseburg, Oregon: what long wet winters and hot Umpqua Valley summers do to older windows, and what a good replacement fixes.
imageAlt: Black-framed Andersen windows and patio doors on a white lap-siding home
body:
Window replacement in Roseburg comes down to two seasons. From fall into spring, windows spend months holding back rain. In summer, the Umpqua Valley turns hot and dry, and the glass on the west side of the house takes the afternoon sun until evening. A good window in Roseburg has to handle both.

We are based in Yoncalla, up I-5 in north Douglas County, and Roseburg is a regular run for us, along with Sutherlin, Winston, Green, and Myrtle Creek. Here is what we see in Roseburg homes and what we recommend.

## What Roseburg Weather Does to Windows

Roseburg sits in climate zone 4C, the marine zone, like most of Western Oregon. Winters are long, gray, and wet. Summers in the valley tend to run a little hotter and drier than they do farther north. That combination is hard on older windows in specific ways:

- **Rot at the sill.** Rain runs down the glass and collects at the bottom of the window. A wood sill that stays wet for months goes soft, and once it does, water finds its way into the wall below.
- **Failed flashing.** Many older homes were never flashed the way a window should be. You cannot see it from inside, but stained drywall under a window or soft siding below it is a common sign.
- **Afternoon heat.** West-facing rooms in July and August can stay hot well into the evening. Old clear glass lets most of that heat straight in.
- **Fogged glass.** Seals on double-pane units wear out from years of daily sun on one side and winter rain sitting against the bottom edge. Once the fog is between the panes, the window cannot be repaired. Our guide to [foggy windows](/blog/foggy-windows-bend-oregon) walks through how to tell what you have.
- **Smoke season.** When wildfire smoke settles into the valley in late summer, loose old sashes let more of it inside.

## What We See in Roseburg Homes

A lot of Roseburg's houses date from the 1950s through the 1990s: single-story ranch homes, split-levels, and older homes near downtown. Many still have their original single-pane aluminum or wood windows, or early double-pane units that have long since lost their seals. Aluminum frames sweat in winter and get hot to the touch in summer. Old wood sashes swell, stick, and get painted shut.

Homes up in the hills around town often have big picture windows facing the view, which are usually the windows that make the living room too cold in January and too warm in August.

None of that means every window has to go. Sometimes a house has a few failing windows on the weather side and the rest are fine. We will tell you which is which.

## What We Recommend

For most Roseburg homes we recommend the [Andersen 100 Series](/andersen). Its Fibrex composite frame does not rot or need paint, is rated twice as strong as vinyl, and holds dark colors without the warping risk that dark vinyl carries in hot sun. With low-E glass, it cuts summer heat gain on west and south walls and keeps winter heat inside. The 2023 Oregon Residential Specialty Code calls for windows at U-0.27 or lower, and the 100 Series meets it.

When a project calls for real wood on the inside, we step up to the Andersen 400 Series. When a quality vinyl window fits your house and budget better, we will tell you that too. We compare frame materials in detail in our [vinyl vs. fiberglass guide](/blog/vinyl-vs-fiberglass-windows-bend-oregon).

The window matters, but in a wet climate the install matters more. We take care with the flashing, the sill, and the seal around every opening, because that is what keeps rain out of the wall for the next twenty years.

## Rebates in Roseburg

Most of Roseburg is served by Pacific Power. Energy Trust of Oregon, which runs efficiency programs for Pacific Power customers, ended its residential window incentives in Oregon at the start of 2026. The federal 25C window tax credit also expired at the end of 2025. So for most Roseburg homeowners, there is no window rebate to count on right now. If a salesperson tells you otherwise, ask them to show you the program in writing.

title: Window Replacement in Eugene, Oregon
excerpt: Window replacement in Eugene, Oregon: rain, moss, hot west-facing rooms, the EWEB window rebate, and what a good replacement fixes in older homes.
imageAlt: Andersen composite-frame replacement window installed in a home
body:
Window replacement in Eugene is mostly about water and sun. From October into spring, rain runs down the glass for weeks at a time. Then summer turns warm and dry, and the west side of the house bakes through the late afternoon. Older windows struggle with both, and plenty of Eugene homes still have the windows they were built with.

We are based in Yoncalla, south of Cottage Grove on I-5, and Eugene is a regular run for us, along with Springfield, Creswell, and Cottage Grove. Here is what we see in Eugene homes, how the EWEB rebate fits in, and what we recommend.

## What Eugene Weather Does to Windows

Eugene sits in climate zone 4C, the marine zone. The winters are mild by temperature and hard by moisture, and that shapes how windows fail here:

- **Rot and soft sills.** Wood sills and lower sash rails that stay wet all winter go soft. Moss and mildew on the north side of the house, especially under big trees, are a sign that side never fully dries out.
- **Failed flashing.** Water that gets past an old window often shows up as staining under the window inside, or soft siding and trim below it outside.
- **Inside condensation.** A house closed up for the wet season holds a lot of moisture, and single-pane or aluminum windows are the coldest surface in the room, so they sweat. Over the years that water damages sills and trim.
- **Hot west rooms.** On summer afternoons, west-facing glass lets in a lot of heat. Low-E glass cuts much of that.
- **Smoke.** In bad smoke years, tight-sealing windows keep more of it outside.

## What We See in Eugene Homes

Eugene has a wide range of houses: older homes near downtown and around the university, post-war and mid-century neighborhoods, 1970s and 1980s split-levels, and hillside homes in the South Hills with big view windows. Many still have single-pane wood windows or aluminum frames from the 1960s and 70s, and a lot of early double-pane windows have lost their seals.

There are also a lot of rentals in Eugene. Landlords replacing windows tend to ask the same things homeowners do: what will hold up, what is easy to maintain, and whether EWEB will help.

Income-qualified homeowners replacing single-pane windows can receive up to $20 per square foot. EWEB also offers zero-interest loans for windows.

Not every project qualifies. Replacing double-pane wood or vinyl windows does not, and neither do windows in garages or unheated spaces. title: EWEB Window Rebate Guide for Eugene Homes
excerpt: Who qualifies for the EWEB window rebate in Eugene, what the $4 and $20 per square foot rebates require, and what does not qualify.
imageAlt: Andersen replacement window installed by Peak View Windows and Doors
body:
If you live in Eugene and EWEB is your electric utility, you may be able to get money back for replacing old windows. It is one of the few window rebates left in Oregon. Energy Trust of Oregon ended its Oregon residential window incentives at the start of 2026, and the federal 25C window tax credit expired at the end of 2025. The EWEB rebate has clear rules, and plenty of homes do not qualify. Here is how it works, in plain terms, so you know where you stand before anyone quotes you. Programs change. Everything below reflects EWEB's published program as of fall 2026. Confirm the current rules with EWEB before you order windows. ## Who Qualifies To qualify for the EWEB window rebate, all of these need to be true: - **You are an EWEB customer.** The account holder, the owner, or someone authorized on the account signs the application. - **Your home is heated mainly with electricity.** EWEB requires primary electric heat serving at least 50% of the home. Electric baseboard, an electric furnace, and a heat pump are typical examples. A home heated mainly with gas or wood does not qualify. - **Your existing windows are single-pane or metal-frame double-pane.** This is the rule that rules out the most homes. Replacing double-pane wood or vinyl windows does not qualify. - **The new windows meet EWEB's efficiency rating.** For the standard rebate, that means a U-factor of 0.22 or lower (glass patio doors at U-0.25 or lower). ## How Much the Rebate Is
ProgramRebateExisting windowsNew window rating
Standard rebate$4 per square foot of glassSingle-pane, or double-pane with metal framesU-0.22 or lower (patio doors U-0.25)
Income-qualified, owner-occupied$20 per square footSingle-pane (including single-pane with storm windows)U-0.30 or lower
Income-qualified, rental$10 per square footSingle-pane (including single-pane with storm windows)U-0.22 or lower (patio doors U-0.25)
The rebate is figured on the square footage of glass, so a house with a lot of big single-pane windows sees more back than a house with a few small ones. EWEB also offers **zero-interest loans** for qualifying window projects, based on your credit history with EWEB. For the standard program, you choose either the rebate or the loan, not both. Income-qualified applicants can combine a rebate and a loan. EWEB publishes the income limits on its website. ## What Does Not Qualify EWEB lists these as not eligible: - Replacing existing double-pane wood or vinyl windows. - Converting a flat window to a garden window. - Making a window opening larger, unless it is for a bedroom egress window. - Windows in garages or other unheated spaces. If your house is heated mainly with gas, or your windows are already double-pane vinyl, the EWEB window rebate will not apply. That does not mean replacing them is a bad idea, only that the rebate is not part of the picture. ## How the Process Works 1. **Check your heat and your windows.** Electric heat as the main system, and single-pane or metal-frame windows. If both are true, keep going. 2. **Get a quote that lists the U-factor for every window.** EWEB needs documentation of each window's rating, such as the window stickers or the manufacturer's order confirmation. Our quotes list the U-factor for every opening. 3. **Talk to EWEB before you order if you are income-qualified.** EWEB's income-qualified program has its own steps, and it is worth calling them first. 4. **Install.** We install, and we keep the window labels and order paperwork EWEB asks for. 5. **Submit the paperwork.** EWEB must receive the installation documentation before it processes any payment. ## The U-0.22 Question The standard rebate's U-0.22 requirement is stricter than Oregon code, which calls for U-0.27 or lower. Not every window line or configuration reaches U-0.22, and the rating can change with the glass package and the window style. A quote that says "energy efficient" without a number is not enough here. If the rebate matters to you, tell us when we come out. We will check the rating on every window we quote and tell you plainly whether it qualifies, so you are not counting on money that will not come. ## What About Springfield and the Rest of Lane County? The EWEB rebate is for EWEB customers. Springfield is served by the Springfield Utility Board, and areas around Eugene are served by other utilities such as EPUD and Lane Electric, each with its own programs. In Douglas County, Roseburg is mostly Pacific Power, where the Energy Trust window incentive has ended. If you are not on EWEB, check with your own utility. ## Worth Doing Even Without a Rebate? Often, yes. Single-pane and old aluminum windows are usually the coldest, wettest, and least comfortable surfaces in a Western Oregon house. We cover the bigger picture in [why new windows pay off in Roseburg and Eugene](/blog/why-replace-windows-bend-oregon) and in our guide to [replacing single-pane windows in older homes](/blog/replace-single-pane-windows-built-before-2000). If you are in Eugene and want to know whether your project fits the EWEB rebate, call 541-639-3968 or [get a free quote](/contact). Clancy will come out, measure, and give you a written quote with the U-factor for every window.

Income-qualified homeowners replacing single-pane windows can receive $20 per square foot, and income-qualified rentals $10 per square foot. Confirm current amounts with EWEB before you order.

title: Replacing Single-Pane Windows in Older Homes
excerpt: Single-pane and old aluminum windows in a pre-2000 home: what they do to comfort in a wet climate, how to tell what you have, and what replacing them fixes.
imageAlt: Window installation by Peak View Windows and Doors
body:
If your home was built before 2000, there is a good chance at least some of its windows are single-pane glass, aluminum frames, or early double-pane units whose seals gave out years ago. Around Roseburg and Eugene, these are the windows we replace most.

They are not always a crisis. Plenty of them still open and close fine. But in a climate with months of cold rain and hot valley summers, they are usually the least comfortable part of the house. Here is how to tell what you have and what replacing it changes.

## How to Tell What Windows You Have

- **Single-pane:** Hold a lighter or a small flashlight near the glass and count the reflections. Each pane of glass makes two, so two reflections means single-pane and four means double-pane. Single-pane glass also feels noticeably colder to the touch on a winter morning.
- **Aluminum frames:** Thin metal frames, often silver or bronze, that feel cold in winter and hot in summer. In older homes these are often sliders.
- **Early double-pane:** Four reflections, but the glass may look hazy between the panes, or the frames may be aluminum. A fogged unit has lost its seal and its insulating gas.
- **Original wood sashes:** Often single-pane, sometimes with storm windows added. Check the sills and the bottom of the sash for soft or dark wood.

## What Old Windows Do in a Western Oregon House

**They sweat.** A single-pane or aluminum window is the coldest surface in the room. In a house closed up for the wet season, indoor moisture condenses on it and runs down to the sill. Over the years that water stains trim, feeds mildew, and rots the wood below the glass.

**They let the heat out, and in.** The U.S. Department of Energy attributes 25 to 30% of a home's heating and cooling energy use to heat moving through windows, and old single-pane glass is the worst of it. In winter you feel a cold draft near the glass even when nothing is technically leaking. In summer, west-facing single-pane glass lets the afternoon heat straight into the room.

**They let water into the wall.** Older windows were often installed with little or no flashing. Decades of wind-driven rain can find its way around the frame and into the wall, which you may not see until the window comes out.

**They let smoke and noise in.** Loose sashes and worn weatherstripping let in more road noise and more wildfire smoke when it settles into the valley.

**They are hard to live with.** Painted-shut sashes, broken balances, and sliders that will not slide. Every bedroom needs a window that opens.

## What Replacing Them Changes

A modern replacement window with low-E insulated glass changes how a room feels more than anything else on this list. The glass on the room side stays much closer to room temperature, so the cold draft and most of the condensation go away. Summer heat through west windows drops. The room gets quieter.

The 2023 Oregon Residential Specialty Code calls for windows rated U-0.27 or lower. For comparison, old single-pane glass is far above that. Ask for the U-factor in writing on any quote.

Replacement is also the chance to fix what the old window was hiding. A full-frame replacement lets us take the old window out, look at the framing, repair soft wood, and flash the opening properly before the new window goes in. That is the part that keeps water out for the next twenty years.

## What We Usually Recommend

For most older homes around Roseburg and Eugene, we recommend the [Andersen 100 Series](/andersen). Its Fibrex composite frame does not rot or need paint, it is rated twice as strong as vinyl, and it comes in styles that suit older houses, including double-hung windows that look right in a traditional home. When you want real wood inside to match existing trim, we step up to the 400 Series. When quality vinyl fits better, we will say so.

## Can You Replace Only Some of Them?

Yes. Many homeowners start with the windows that bother them most: the cold bedroom, the sweating kitchen window, the west-facing living room. We will tell you which windows are failing and which can wait. Doing the worst side of the house first is a reasonable plan.

## Rebates for Single-Pane Windows

In Eugene, EWEB customers with electric heat who are replacing single-pane or metal-frame windows may qualify for a rebate. Our [EWEB window rebate guide](/blog/eweb-window-rebate-eugene-oregon) explains who qualifies. Energy Trust of Oregon ended its Oregon window incentives at the start of 2026, and the federal 25C window tax credit expired at the end of 2025, so outside EWEB territory there is usually no rebate right now.

## The Short Version

If your home has single-pane glass, aluminum frames, or fogged early double-pane windows, they are probably making the house less comfortable every winter and every summer, and they may be letting water into the wall. Replacing them with a well-installed, low-E window fixes the cold draft, most of the condensation, and a lot of the summer heat.

If you want to know which of your windows need replacing and which can stay, call 541-639-3968 or [get a free quote](/contact). Clancy will come out, measure, check the sills, and give you a written quote.

faq.a: Single-pane and aluminum windows are the coldest surface in the room, so indoor moisture condenses on them, especially in a house closed up for the wet season. Better ventilation helps, but the lasting fix is insulated low-E glass, which keeps the room-side glass much warmer.

title: Pella Impervia Windows in Roseburg & Eugene
excerpt: Are Pella Impervia fiberglass windows worth it for a Roseburg or Eugene home? An honest look at where the line wins, where it doesn't, and who should skip it.
imageAlt: A replacement window installed by Peak View Windows and Doors
body:
Pella Impervia fiberglass windows hold up well to daily heating and cooling because fiberglass expands and contracts at close to the same rate as the glass it holds, which puts less stress on the seal than a more reactive frame does. Fiberglass also does not rot or soak up water. That makes it a strong option for a dark exterior color and a long ownership horizon in a wet climate. It is not automatically the right choice for every house. The color list is shorter than painted wood, it is a step up from vinyl, and it is a smaller category with fewer stock configurations and sometimes longer lead times. We have covered the [broader vinyl vs. fiberglass vs. composite vs. wood question](/blog/vinyl-vs-fiberglass-windows-bend-oregon) already. This post goes narrow: is Impervia worth a look for a house in Roseburg or Eugene, and for whom? ## What Is Fiberglass as a Frame Material, and Why Does It Matter Here? Fiberglass window frames are woven glass fibers set in resin, formed into the frame and sash. The property that matters is how little the material moves as temperature changes. Fiberglass moves much closer to the rate of glass than vinyl does. Vinyl can move several times more across the same heat-cold swing, according to comparison data compiled by This Old House. In Western Oregon that matters in two ways. First, the daily cycle on a sunny wall: a west-facing frame goes from a cool morning to hours of direct summer sun and back again. A frame that moves a lot stresses the seal on every cycle, and over enough years that is how seals fail and glass fogs. Second, the wet months. Fiberglass does not absorb water, swell, or rot, so it does not care how many weeks in a row it rains. ## What Does Pella Say About Impervia? Pella markets Impervia as its fiberglass line, built around a proprietary fiberglass composite the company calls Duracast. Pella's product materials claim the material has been tested across a range from -40°F to 180°F without warping or sagging. Those are Pella's own claims about its own product, and we pass them along as Pella's claims, not as independently verified fact. On the exterior, Pella describes Impervia's finish as a heavy-duty powder coat that it says resists chipping, chalking, and fading, and that meets a fiberglass-coating industry standard (AAMA 624). According to Pella, that is why the company does not recommend repainting the frame over its life. Pella offers Impervia in a limited set of factory finishes rather than an open paint palette, including a dual-color option with a white interior and a choice of exterior colors, black among them. It comes in most of the styles a full-house replacement needs: double-hung, single-hung, casement, awning, sliding, and picture windows, plus some patio door configurations. Pella backs Impervia with what it calls a Limited Lifetime Warranty, with different terms depending on the component and whether the original buyer still owns the home. Read Pella's actual warranty document before you buy, and ask whoever quotes it to walk you through what is covered. ## Does Fiberglass Hold Up Better in Dark Colors? Black and other dark exteriors are some of the most requested finishes we quote, and dark color is where frame material stops being cosmetic and becomes a performance choice. Dark surfaces absorb more solar heat than light ones. On a material that already moves a lot with temperature, that heat makes warping a real risk, which is why some vinyl manufacturers build heat-reflective layers into their darker colors. Fiberglass does not eliminate heat gain. A black fiberglass frame still gets hotter in the sun than a white one. What changes is how much that heat makes the frame move. Because fiberglass already moves close to the rate of glass, a dark finish does not push it into the kind of movement that warps more reactive materials. That is the real reason we point homeowners toward fiberglass or composite when they want a dark exterior and plan to stay for decades. ## Fiberglass vs. Vinyl vs. Composite, at a Glance
FactorFiberglassVinylComposite (Fibrex)
Movement with heat and coldLowest; close to glassHighest of the threeLow; manufacturer rates it far more stable than vinyl
Dark colors in summer sunStrong; little added warping riskWeakest in dark colors unless the product is built for itColor runs through the material; holds dark finishes well
Wet-weather durabilityDoes not absorb water or rotDoes not rotPolymer-encased wood fiber resists rot and swelling
Strength and sightlinesStiff and light; supports narrower framesSofter; needs thicker frame walls for the same spanRated well above vinyl for rigidity
Color optionsA defined set of factory finishesWidest range of stock colorsDefined factory finishes

## Where Fiberglass Wins - **Low frame movement.** Less stress on the glazing seal over thousands of heat-cold cycles than a more reactive frame. - **Indifferent to rain.** Fiberglass does not swell, rot, or soak up water through a long wet season. - **Dark colors without the added warping risk** that comes with heat-reactive materials. - **Slimmer sightlines for the same strength.** More glass, less frame, in the same opening. - **A finish that is not a paint film.** Pella's powder coat on Impervia is baked on, so there is no repainting cycle. - **A long expected life.** Fiberglass as a category commonly lasts decades longer than standard vinyl, which matters if you are staying in the house. ## Where Fiberglass, and Impervia Specifically, Does Not Win This is the part a brochure will not lead with, so we will. - **Color options are narrower than painted wood.** If you need to match a specific custom exterior color, or want the option to repaint later, painted wood or clad-wood gives you that flexibility and fiberglass does not. - **It is a step up from vinyl**, and usually from composite lines like Andersen's Fibrex as well. If what you need is a light or mid-tone exterior on a standard-size opening and your budget is tight, a quality vinyl window installed correctly is a good answer, and we will tell you that plainly. ## Is Fiberglass Right for Your House? A Quick Checklist - You want a dark exterior color (black, charcoal, deep bronze) and do not want to worry about heat-related warping. - You plan to own the home for 20-plus years and want a frame that is still doing its job in year 30. - You have larger openings where a narrower frame and more glass matter to the look of the room. - You are not trying to match a custom-painted exterior color. - Your budget has room for a step up from vinyl and, in most cases, from composite as well. - Your timeline can flex for a smaller-category product. title: Vinyl vs Fibrex Windows for Roseburg & Eugene
excerpt: Vinyl vs Fibrex windows for a Roseburg or Eugene home: how each handles rain, summer sun, and dark colors, and when vinyl is the smarter buy.
imageAlt: Andersen 100 Series Fibrex composite windows framing a living room view
body:
Vinyl vs Fibrex windows comes down to one mechanical question: how much does the frame move as it heats and cools, and what does that movement do to the seal over twenty or thirty years? Andersen builds Fibrex, the composite in its 100 Series, to move less than vinyl through that cycle, and bases its claims of longer-lasting dark colors and tighter seals on that difference. Vinyl moves more, but modern vinyl is engineered around that movement, is easier on the budget, and is a good window for the right house. Neither is a wrong answer. The right one depends on your color choice, your budget, and how long you plan to own the house. ## What Is Fibrex, Actually? Fibrex is not vinyl with a different name. Andersen states that Fibrex is a composite of reclaimed wood fiber combined with thermoplastic polymer, with each wood fiber encased in the polymer during manufacturing. Wood fiber adds rigidity and stability, while the polymer coating shields it from moisture so it cannot rot, swell, or soak up water the way bare wood would. In a Western Oregon winter, that matters. Andersen holds the patent on Fibrex and is the only manufacturer that makes it, so it is not an industry-wide category like vinyl or fiberglass. That means a shorter field history than materials many manufacturers have run for decades, and you cannot comparison-shop it across brands. ## What Modern Vinyl Actually Is Vinyl gets treated like the bargain option by default, and that reputation is out of date. Vinyl frames are extruded rigid PVC, built with hollow internal chambers that trap air for insulation. In a quality vinyl window the color is mixed into the PVC before extrusion, so it runs through the full thickness of the frame rather than sitting on top as paint. The corners are heat-welded, not screwed or glued. A properly fusion-welded joint is stronger than the surrounding vinyl and forms a continuous, watertight seal around the sash. That detail is worth asking about on any vinyl quote. It separates a well-built window from a poorly built one more than the word "vinyl" on the spec sheet does. Vinyl does not rot and never needs paint, which is a real point in its favor in a rainy climate. ## Why Frame Movement Is the Real Story We have written about [what our wet winters and hot valley summers do to windows](/blog/why-replace-windows-bend-oregon) in general. For frame material, thermal expansion is the mechanism behind most of what follows. Every frame grows slightly when it heats and shrinks when it cools. What matters is how much a given length of material moves per degree. Vinyl moves notably more than Fibrex across the same change. Our yearly temperature range is milder than inland Oregon's, but the daily cycle on a sunny wall is real: a west-facing frame goes from a cool morning to hours of direct afternoon sun and back, every clear day from June to September. That repeated cycling is what wears a window out. Not one hot day, but thousands of small movements over decades. Each cycle flexes the seal between sash and glass a tiny amount, and a seal stressed enough times eventually fails, letting moisture between the panes. Fibrex's lower movement is the whole argument for it here: less movement, less cumulative stress. That does not mean vinyl fails here. Quality vinyl is engineered with expansion joints and tolerances that account for this movement. It is doing more work to manage a bigger problem, while Fibrex has less problem to manage in the first place. ## Dark Colors and Summer Sun Black-on-black is one of the most requested finishes we quote, and it is the hardest test for any frame. Dark colors absorb more solar energy than light ones, and a dark frame in direct afternoon sun can run dramatically hotter than a white frame next to it. On a hot valley afternoon, a west-facing black frame is working hard. That heat drives expansion, so a dark frame moves more than a light frame of the same material. That is why unmodified dark vinyl has a history of softening and warping in strong sun. Some vinyl manufacturers now bond a heat-reflective outer layer over a lighter core to manage a dark exterior. If you want a dark vinyl frame, ask what specific feature the product uses. "Dark vinyl" and "dark vinyl engineered for it" are not the same window. Fibrex, according to Andersen, resists that warping because the wood fiber keeps the material more stable as it heats, and the color is mixed through the material so it does not need repainting. Worth saying plainly: we cannot independently verify decades of field performance on a material only Andersen makes. ## Strength and Sightlines How much glass you get in an opening depends on how thin the frame can be while still holding the sash rigid. A stiffer material lets a manufacturer build a narrower profile for the same job. Andersen states Fibrex tests twice as strong as extruded vinyl. Vinyl makes up for being softer with thicker frame walls and internal chambers, part of why vinyl sightlines generally run chunkier than Fibrex at a comparable size. For most rooms this matters less than color and budget, but on a wall that looks out at the trees and hills, it is a real, visible difference. ## Where Fibrex Falls Short Fibrex ships in a defined set of factory finishes rather than the open palette of painted wood, which is a real limit if you are matching an unusual exterior color. It is a newer material than vinyl or wood: Andersen has decades of its own exposure data, but that is one manufacturer's data on one product, not the multi-manufacturer track record vinyl and wood have. And it is a step up from entry-level vinyl, which buys the lower movement and higher strength above, but is not worth it on every project. ## Vinyl vs. Fibrex: Side by Side
VinylFibrex (Andersen 100 Series)
Movement with heat and cold: Higher; quality lines engineer around it with expansion joints and tolerancesMovement with heat and cold: Lower per Andersen; less daily movement, less cumulative seal stress
Dark colors in sun: Dark exteriors run hottest; ask if the product uses a heat-reflective outer layerDark colors in sun: Andersen states the wood-fiber content resists warping under heat; color runs through the material
Wet weather: Does not rot or absorb waterWet weather: Polymer-encased wood fiber resists rot and swelling
Strength and sightlines: Softer; needs thicker frame walls for the same spanStrength and sightlines: Andersen rates it twice the strength of vinyl, allowing a narrower frame
Color options: Wide range across many manufacturersColor options: Defined factory palette from one manufacturer
Maintenance: No painting; occasional cleaningMaintenance: No painting; occasional cleaning, per Andersen
Track record: Decades of multi-manufacturer field historyTrack record: Andersen cites over 30 years of exposure testing; shorter independent history
## Which One Fits Your House? - **Light or mid exterior color, standard-size openings, budget matters most:** quality vinyl is a good call. Put the difference into a better installer, not a fancier frame. - **You want black or another dark exterior and plan to stay long-term:** Fibrex's lower movement under heat is the reason it earns the step up for this use. - **You want a narrow sightline to get more glass on a view wall:** Fibrex's added strength supports a thinner frame for the same opening. - **You are replacing a window or two on a tight budget:** a well-built vinyl window, installed and flashed correctly, holds up fine here. Neither material is the safe or the risky choice across the board. If you want the [Andersen 100 Series](/andersen) quoted side by side with a quality vinyl option for your actual windows, we will walk the house, measure every opening, and give you both quotes in writing so you can compare them honestly. Call 541-639-3968 or [request a free quote online](/contact). No pressure either way.

faq.q: Is Fibrex better than vinyl for windows?
faq.a: Neither is better in every situation. Fibrex, the composite Andersen uses in its 100 Series, moves less than vinyl as temperatures change and, according to Andersen, holds dark colors and strength better over time. Vinyl moves more but is engineered to handle it, is easier on the budget, and is a solid choice for light or mid-colored windows. The right answer depends on your exterior color and how long you plan to own the home.

faq.q: What is Fibrex made of?
faq.a: Andersen states that Fibrex is a composite of reclaimed wood fiber and thermoplastic polymer, with each wood fiber encased in the polymer during manufacturing. Andersen holds the patent on the material, is the only manufacturer that produces it, and uses it in the Andersen 100 Series.

faq.q: Do black window frames warp in the sun?
faq.a: Dark colors absorb more solar heat than light colors, and that heat drives expansion and warping risk. This is a bigger concern for vinyl, where some manufacturers use a heat-reflective outer layer over a lighter core to manage dark colors. Ask what feature a vinyl product uses if you want a dark exterior. Andersen states Fibrex resists this kind of warping because of its wood-fiber content, though that claim comes from the one manufacturer that makes it.

faq.q: Is vinyl a good window material or only the bargain option?
faq.a: Modern quality vinyl is a good window material. It is rigid PVC with color mixed through the material, built with insulating internal chambers and heat-welded corners that form a strong, watertight seal. It does not rot or need paint. For a standard-size opening in a light or mid exterior color, a well-built vinyl window installed correctly is a smart, durable choice.

faq.q: Do Fibrex or vinyl windows rot in a wet climate?
faq.a: Neither one rots the way a bare wood frame or sill can. Vinyl is solid PVC, and Fibrex encases its wood fiber in polymer so it does not soak up water. In Western Oregon the bigger risk is the install: a window that is not flashed and sealed properly lets water into the wall below it, whatever the frame is made of.

title: Comparing Window Quotes in Roseburg & Eugene
excerpt: Why two honest window quotes on the same Roseburg or Eugene house can look nothing alike, and what to check line by line before you compare them.
imageAlt: Window installation by Peak View Windows and Doors
body:
Two honest contractors can quote the same house and hand you two quotes that look nothing alike. Usually neither one is wrong. They quoted two different jobs. A window quote bundles a dozen separate decisions into one page: frame material, glass, whether the whole frame comes out or only the sash, what happens if there is rot at the sill, and what the trim looks like afterward. Two contractors rarely bundle them the same way. This guide is about reading what is inside each quote, so that when you compare them you are comparing the same work. ## Why Two Quotes for the Same House Look So Different One quote might include full-frame replacement, new flashing, trim restoration, haul-away of the old windows, and a written labor warranty. Another might quote an insert into the existing frame, skip the trim, and leave rot repair as a change order if it turns up mid-project. Both are technically "a quote for windows." They are not the same job. In Western Oregon the biggest hidden difference is usually water. Plenty of homes around Roseburg and Eugene have wood sills that have been taking rain for decades, and flashing that was never right to begin with. A quote that addresses that and a quote that does not can look very far apart, and the one that ignores it is not doing you a favor. The fix is not chasing the smallest number on the page. It is asking what each quote includes before you put them side by side. ## What Changes From One Quote to the Next
What to compareWhat can differ between quotesWhy it matters
Frame material and product lineVinyl, fiberglass, composite, or clad-wood, and which manufacturer and seriesTwo "vinyl windows" from different lines are not the same window
Glass packageLow-E coating, gas fill, warm-edge spacers, and the U-factor that resultsThis decides most of the energy performance and how the room feels in summer sun
Full-frame vs. insertWhether the old frame is removed and the opening rebuilt, or a new unit is set inside the old frameInsert reuses whatever condition the old frame is in, good or bad
Rot and flashingWhether the quote says how sill rot and failed flashing will be handled if foundIn a wet climate this is where the biggest surprises live
Interior and exterior trimRestored, replaced, or left as isFinish carpentry decides how the job looks for the next 20 years
Operation typeFixed, double-hung, casement, or slider for each openingChanging the style changes the window, and sometimes egress for a bedroom
Hard-access openingsSecond-story or tight openings that need stagingSome quotes include it; some add it later
Haul-away and cleanupIncluded or separateSmall line, easy to miss
WarrantyProduct warranty and labor warranty, in writingA product warranty does not cover a bad install
Lead time and scheduleManufacturer lead time and an install date rangeCustom sizes and some lines take longer to build
## Full-Frame vs. Insert: The Choice Behind Most of the Gap Insert replacement, sometimes called pocket replacement, keeps your existing frame and sets a new window unit inside it. Full-frame replacement removes the old window down to the framing, looks at what is behind it, and rebuilds the opening from there, including the flashing. Insert replacement is not automatically wrong. If the existing frame is square, dry, and solid, it is a legitimate, less invasive option. But that only holds if the frame really is sound, and in a house that has seen decades of Western Oregon rain, the only way to know is to look. A contractor who recommends inserts for every opening without checking the sills may be avoiding a conversation about what they would find. The energy side of the glass question is worth its own read. We cover what a window upgrade does for comfort and energy bills in [why new windows pay off in Roseburg and Eugene](/blog/why-replace-windows-bend-oregon). ## What a Quote Cannot See Until the Old Window Comes Out No contractor can see through your siding. Rot around a sill, a window that was never flashed properly, or water damage in the framing below only shows up once the old unit comes out. That is why a quote with no language about what happens if they find a problem is worth a second look. "We will not know until we open it up, and here is how we will handle it if we find something" is an honest quote. A flat number with no plan for surprises usually means nobody has told you yet. ## What Your Quote Should Spell Out A quote you can compare against another one should state, in writing: 1. The product line and series, not only "vinyl window," but the manufacturer and model. 2. The U-factor for every window. The 2023 Oregon Residential Specialty Code calls for U-0.27 or lower, and a real quote states it. 3. Full-frame or insert, specified per opening, not one blanket line for the whole house. 4. How the opening will be flashed and sealed, and how rot will be handled if it is found. 5. What happens to interior and exterior trim on each opening: restored, replaced, or left alone. 6. Whether haul-away of the old windows is included. 7. The manufacturer's estimated lead time and an install date range. 8. Warranty terms for both the product and the labor. 9. A clear total and payment schedule, not a monthly payment with no total attached. 10. Who will actually be at your house doing the work. With us, Clancy is on every job. ## Red Flags Worth Slowing Down For - No U-factor anywhere in the paperwork. - A deal that disappears if you do not sign before the salesperson leaves. - Financing shown only as a monthly payment, with no total anywhere. - A single lump-sum number with no line-item scope behind it. - No mention of flashing or sill repair on a house with obviously old wood windows. - Nobody can tell you who will be doing the install. Today's Homeowner's rundown of window-company red flags lines up with this. Pressure to put down a deposit immediately, and "limited-time" deals that only hold if you sign right now, are two of the clearest signs a quote was built to be signed under pressure rather than compared honestly. ## Get a Real Quote for Your House The only quote that means anything is one written against your actual openings after someone has measured them and looked at the sills. We will come do that: a free in-home quote, everything in writing, and no pressure to sign the same day. Call 541-639-3968 or [request a free quote](/contact).

faq.q: Why did two contractors quote my house so differently?
faq.a: Almost always because they quoted different jobs, not because one is out of line. One quote may include full-frame replacement, new flashing, trim restoration, haul-away, and a labor warranty; another may quote an insert with no trim work and leave rot repair as a change order. Ask each contractor to spell out exactly what is included per opening before comparing them.

faq.q: What is the difference between insert and full-frame window replacement?
faq.a: Insert replacement keeps your existing frame and sets a new window inside it. Full-frame replacement removes the old window down to the framing and rebuilds the opening, including the flashing. Insert is a good option when the old frame is square, dry, and solid. Full-frame is the honest answer when the sill has rot, the window was never flashed correctly, or the frame is out of square.

faq.q: What should a window replacement quote include?
faq.a: The product line and series, the U-factor for each window, full-frame or insert for each opening, how flashing and any rot will be handled, what happens to the trim, haul-away, lead time and install dates, product and labor warranties, a clear total, and who will be doing the work.

faq.q: How long does it take to get new windows once I order them?
faq.a: Manufacturer lead times typically run a few weeks depending on the product line and how custom the sizes are, and custom shapes or specialty lines tend to run longer. We give you the expected lead time and an install date range in writing with your quote.

faq.q: What should I do before getting window replacement quotes?
faq.a: Walk your house and note which windows bother you and why: drafty, fogged, rotting at the sill, painted shut, or hard to open. Count them. That list lets you compare quotes on the same scope, because the fastest way for two quotes to drift apart is for each contractor to assume a different set of windows and a different depth of work.

title: Vinyl vs. Fiberglass Windows for Western Oregon
excerpt: Vinyl vs. fiberglass windows for wet winters and hot valley summers: the real trade-offs, and when quality vinyl is the smarter buy.
imageAlt: Black-framed Andersen 100 Series casement window with a composite frame
body:
Vinyl vs. fiberglass windows comes down to one real trade-off. Fiberglass and Andersen's Fibrex composite move less as the temperature changes and hold dark colors better over the decades. Modern quality vinyl does the job well and is easier on the budget. Neither is the wrong answer. In Roseburg and Eugene, the honest way to choose is to ask three questions: which frame moves the least, which one shrugs off months of rain, and which one handles a dark color in hot valley sun. Not which one looks best in a showroom. ## Why Frame Movement Matters Here We have covered [why our wet winters and hot valley summers are hard on old windows](/blog/why-replace-windows-bend-oregon) in general. For frame material, the question is narrower. Every frame material expands when it heats and contracts when it cools. What matters is how much, and what that movement does to the seal holding the glass. A frame that moves a lot stresses that seal on every cycle. Do that every day for fifteen years and the seal eventually fails, which is the fogged-glass problem that cannot be repaired, only replaced. Our yearly temperature range is milder than inland Oregon's. The daily cycle is not. A west-facing frame in August goes from a cool morning to full afternoon sun and back again, and a dark frame in that sun gets far hotter than the air around it. Then the rain comes, and the frame spends months wet. That is the test every material below has to pass. ## Vinyl Windows: The Honest Case For and Against Vinyl is PVC, a thermoplastic, and the most temperature-reactive of the common frame materials. This Old House reports vinyl's movement with heat and cold runs more than twice that of aluminum, wood, and fiberglass, and roughly seven times that of the glass it holds. Good vinyl windows are engineered around that movement with expansion joints and design tolerances. It shows up most in dark colors. Dark finishes absorb more solar heat, and that heat drives vinyl's warping risk. Window manufacturer Ply Gem describes the mechanism on its own black-vinyl product page. Some manufacturers now build a heat-reflective outer layer over a lighter core to manage it. If you want a dark vinyl exterior, ask what feature the product uses. Vinyl is also softer than fiberglass or composite, so frames need thicker walls for the same glass span, which is why vinyl sightlines run chunkier at a comparable size. None of that makes vinyl a bad choice. Vinyl does not rot, it does not need paint, and in a wet climate that counts for a lot. A light or mid-colored vinyl window from a reputable line, installed correctly, commonly lasts 20 to 30 years, per This Old House. For a standard-size opening in a light color, quality vinyl is a good window. The trade-off is specific: more movement, a real limit on how dark you can go, and a shorter typical life than fiberglass at the top end. ## Fiberglass Windows: Where the Step Up Goes Fiberglass frames are woven glass fibers set in resin, so they expand and contract at close to the same rate as the glass panes inside them. This Old House's comparison found fiberglass moves far less than vinyl across a heat-cold cycle. That lower movement is the whole argument for fiberglass: less stress on the glazing seal, cycle after cycle. Fiberglass is also stiffer than vinyl, which lets manufacturers build narrower frames for the same strength. More glass, less frame, in the same opening. Because it moves less when it heats up, dark fiberglass frames are less prone to warping, and fiberglass does not absorb water or rot. The trade-off is that fiberglass is a clear step up from vinyl, and it is a smaller category, with fewer manufacturers, fewer stock configurations, and sometimes longer lead times. In exchange, fiberglass commonly lasts 30 to 50 years against vinyl's 20 to 30. It earns its place for someone staying put for decades. ## Composite (Andersen Fibrex): The Middle Ground Fibrex is Andersen's own material, not generic vinyl or fiberglass. It is a composite of reclaimed wood fiber and thermoplastic polymer. Andersen contrasts it directly with vinyl: where vinyl can expand in the sun and contract in the cold, Fibrex retains its stability and rigidity, and Andersen rates it twice as strong as vinyl. The polymer encases the wood fiber, so it does not rot or swell in our wet months. Like vinyl, the color runs through the material rather than sitting on top as paint. Andersen backs it with more than 30 years of field exposure, including Minnesota test windows the company reports show no cracking, rotting, or peeling after three decades. That is a real track record, though worth saying plainly: Fibrex is a newer category than fiberglass or wood. This is the [Andersen 100 Series](/andersen) we install most often, and black-on-black is one of the most requested combinations we quote. The real trade-offs are a shorter color list than painted wood and a step up from most vinyl. ## Wood and Clad-Wood: When It Is Still Worth It Solid wood moves with humidity and temperature the way it always has, and in Western Oregon humidity is the bigger of the two. A clad-wood window wraps the outside in a protective shell, usually vinyl or aluminum, so the wood stays inside where it is dry and the cladding takes the weather. How well that holds up depends almost entirely on the cladding and how it is sealed at the corners and sill. The Efficient Windows Collaborative notes wood-polymer composite claddings are engineered for better moisture and decay resistance than bare wood. Heavier extruded cladding outlasts thin roll-formed cladding, which is a fair question to ask on any quote. A well-built, well-maintained clad-wood window commonly reaches 25 to 40 years and beyond, but "well-maintained" is doing real work. The interior finish needs upkeep the other three materials do not ask for, and any break in the cladding lets water reach the wood. It is the right call when you are matching real wood trim already in the house. ## Vinyl vs. Fiberglass vs. Composite vs. Wood: Side by Side
MaterialMovement with heat and coldDark colors in summer sunWet-weather durabilityTypical lifespan
VinylHighest of the fourRuns hottest in dark colors; ask how the product manages heatDoes not rot or need paint20 to 30 years
FiberglassLowest; close to the rate of glassBest dark-color stability of the fourDoes not absorb water or rot30 to 50 years
Composite (Fibrex)Low; Andersen rates it far more stable than vinylColor runs through the material; won't peel or flakePolymer-encased wood fiber resists rot and swelling20 to 30+ years (newer material)
Wood / clad-woodWood core moves with humidity; cladding shields itDepends on cladding and finish qualityGood while the cladding stays sealed; wood rots if water gets in25 to 40+ years with upkeep
## Questions to Ask About Frame Material on Any Quote - **What is the frame material, specifically?** Ask for the manufacturer and line name, not only the category. - **What is the whole-window U-factor?** The 2023 Oregon Residential Specialty Code calls for U-0.27 or lower, whatever the frame. - **If you want a dark exterior, how does this product manage heat?** A real answer names a feature, not a general reassurance. - **Does the color warranty change for dark colors?** Coverage terms are not always the same as standard colors. - **How is the sill flashed and sealed?** In our climate this matters as much as the frame material. - **What is the lead time?** Composite and fiberglass lines commonly run longer than mainstream vinyl. ## Which Frame Material Should You Choose? - **Standard-size openings, a light or mid exterior color, a tighter budget:** quality vinyl is a good choice. Put the difference into a better installer, not a fancier frame. - **You want black or another dark exterior and plan to own the home 20-plus years:** fiberglass or Fibrex composite earns the step up by not fighting the color you want in summer sun. - **You need a real wood interior to match existing millwork:** clad-wood, planned honestly for the upkeep it asks for. - **You are replacing one or two windows:** quality vinyl installed correctly beats any frame installed poorly. None of these materials is the wrong answer, and we will say so plainly if vinyl is what fits your house. If you want us to walk your windows and tell you which material fits your openings, colors, and budget, we will come to your home for a free quote and give you a firm, itemized quote in writing. No showroom, no pressure. Call 541-639-3968 or [request a free quote online](/contact).

Both resist rot in our wet winters. Quality vinyl performs well here too, especially in light or mid exterior colors, and it is easier on the budget. Fiberglass and Andersen's Fibrex composite move less when they heat up, so dark colors are less risky on those materials. If you want a dark vinyl frame, ask what feature the product uses to manage heat.

faq.q: Is fiberglass a big step up from vinyl?
faq.a: Fiberglass sits above vinyl, and that ordering is consistent across every published survey. How big the step is depends on the line, the size of your openings, and the glass package, which is why we quote your actual windows instead of pointing at an average. Get it in writing for your specific windows rather than relying on a rule of thumb.

faq.q: What is Andersen's Fibrex, and is it the same as vinyl?
faq.a: Fibrex is Andersen's own composite material, made from reclaimed wood fiber combined with thermoplastic polymer. It is not the same as generic vinyl. Andersen rates Fibrex as twice as strong as vinyl and says it resists the expansion and contraction Andersen identifies as a weakness in standard vinyl. It is the material in the Andersen 100 Series, the line we install most often.

faq.q: How long do vinyl windows last in a wet climate?
faq.a: A quality vinyl window installed correctly commonly lasts 20 to 30 years, per This Old House. Vinyl does not rot, which helps in Western Oregon, but the install matters a great deal here: a window that is not flashed and sealed properly lets water into the wall no matter what the frame is made of.

title: Foggy Windows in Roseburg & Eugene, Explained
excerpt: Cloudy glass can be a free humidity fix or a failed seal. How to tell which one you have in 60 seconds, written for wet Western Oregon winters.
body:
A foggy window means one of three things, and only one of them means buying anything. Condensation on the inside of the glass is an indoor humidity problem. Condensation on the outside on a cool morning usually means the window is doing its job. A permanent haze between the two panes means the seal on that insulated glass unit has failed. That third case is the only one you cannot clean away. Foggy windows are one of the most common calls we get from Roseburg and Eugene homeowners once the rain settles in each fall, so here is how to tell the three apart in about sixty seconds, and what fixes each one. ## Condensation on the Inside of the Glass: Almost Always Humidity If the fog is on the room side of the glass and wipes away with a finger, your window is not the problem. As Andersen Windows explains in its own condensation guide, condensation forms inside a window because indoor humidity is too high for the glass temperature, not because something is wrong with the window. Western Oregon homes hold a lot of moisture in winter. The house is closed up for months, the air outside is damp, and showers, cooking, laundry, houseplants, and a family breathing overnight all add more. A tightly built or newly sealed home keeps that moisture in instead of leaking it out the way a drafty old house did. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency recommends keeping indoor relative humidity in roughly the 30 to 40 percent range in winter to help avoid this kind of condensation. The fix is usually free: run the bathroom fan longer after a shower, vent the kitchen hood and dryer outside, and add a dehumidifier to a damp room or a daylight basement. Even on a rainy day, cold outside air holds less moisture than warm indoor air, so a little ventilation still helps. Left alone for years, ProVia notes that moisture can work into the wood trim around a window and lead to mold and rot. In a climate this wet, that is the real reason to take it seriously. ## Condensation on the Outside of the Glass: Usually a Sign the Window Is Working If the fog or dew is on the outside of the glass and only shows up on cool, clear, still mornings, that is not a defect. It is often a sign your low-E glass is doing exactly what it should. Modern low-E coatings hold indoor heat in so well that the outer pane runs colder than it would on an older, leakier window. On a calm fall or spring morning in the valley, that cold surface can drop below the dew point, and moisture in the air condenses on it the same way it beads up on a cold glass of water. Andersen Windows puts it plainly: condensation on the outside of a window is a sign of energy efficiency. ProVia makes the same point. It needs no fix and usually burns off once the sun reaches the glass. Homeowners who recently upgraded sometimes see this for the first time and assume something is wrong. It is the upgrade working. ## Moisture Between the Panes: The One That Does Not Wipe Away This is the case that needs a real fix. If the haze sits between the two panes, sometimes with a faint rainbow sheen, a streaky film, or a chalky white line along the edge, no amount of cleaning touches it, because you cannot reach it. Insulated glass units are a sealed sandwich: two panes of glass, a gap filled with insulating gas (usually argon), and a perimeter seal holding it together. When that edge seal breaks down, the gas leaks out and moist outside air leaks in. That moisture condenses on the inner glass surfaces, sealed away from any rag. Andersen Windows is direct about it: once the seal breaks and condensation forms between the panes, you will not be able to stop it, and replacement is the real solution. It is not only cosmetic. The National Renewable Energy Laboratory, which studies insulating glass, has found that a failed seal can raise a unit's U-factor by as much as 32 percent. In bad cases the window performs close to single-pane glass. You will find "defogging" services that drill a small hole in the glass, flush out the moisture, and reseal it. Per Angi's reporting on the practice, it is a cosmetic fix. It does not restore the lost gas or repair the broken seal, and the fog commonly returns within a year or two. Treat it as a way to buy time, not a permanent answer.
Where the fog isWhat it meansWhat fixes itDo you need new glass?
Inside surface of the glassIndoor humidity is too high for the glass temperatureVentilation, exhaust fans, or a dehumidifierNo
Outside surface, mornings onlyLow-E glass is keeping heat inside so well that the outer pane runs coldNothing. It clears once the sun reaches the glassNo
Between the panes, permanent haze or filmThe insulated glass unit's seal has failed and the gas fill is goneA glass-only swap if the frame is sound; a full window if it is notYes. We look at the frame and tell you which fix fits
## Why Seals Fail on Western Oregon Homes An insulated glass seal flexes every day. The sun warms the gas inside the unit and it expands; the night cools it and it contracts. Thompson Creek, a national window manufacturer, notes that south- and west-facing windows commonly fail five to ten years earlier than north-facing windows on the same house, because they take the most direct sun and the biggest daily swings. In the valley, that is the glass taking the hot summer afternoons. Water is the other half of the story here. Edge seals are built to stay dry. On an older window with failed glazing putty, a cracked bead, or clogged weep holes, rain that runs down the glass all winter can sit against the bottom edge of the unit for weeks. Months of standing water on a seal, year after year, wears it out faster than sun alone. Fall is a good time to go look. Every seal in the house has been through a hot summer, and the first cold, wet weeks are when a failing unit starts to show it. ## A 60-Second Checklist for Foggy Windows 1. **Look at it in daylight.** Does the haze sit on the surface, like it might wipe off, or does it look trapped inside the glass, maybe with a rainbow sheen or a white line at the edge? 2. **Wipe the inside pane.** If the moisture comes off with a dry cloth and the glass underneath is clear, that is surface condensation, not a seal failure. 3. **Note which side and what time of day.** Outside fog that only appears on cool, clear mornings and burns off by mid-morning is dew. Inside fog after cooking or showering, or once the house is closed up for winter, is humidity. 4. **Check whether it ever fully clears.** Surface condensation comes and goes with the weather. A failed seal does not. The haze is there in July the same as January. 5. **Check the sill while you are there.** Press the wood below the glass. If it feels soft or looks dark and stained, water has been getting in, and that changes what the right fix is. 6. **Walk the rest of the house.** One hazy window is a single failed unit. Several fogging the same way often means a batch of units reaching the end of their life together. ## Repair or Replace: The Honest Version If what you have is inside or outside surface condensation, you do not need a window company. You need better ventilation or a little patience with the morning sun. We will tell you that for free if you send us a photo. If it is a failed seal, the right fix depends on the rest of the window: - **Frame and hardware still solid, one unit gone bad:** a glass-only swap, pulling the failed sealed unit and setting a new one into the existing sash, is usually the simplest real fix, and often all you need. - **Sash warped, balances failing, or an odd older size:** replacing the sash or the whole unit makes more sense than fighting a frame that is already going. - **Rot in the frame or sill, or several windows failing at once:** full-frame replacement is worth it. That lets us open the wall, fix the flashing, and seal the opening properly. It is where we usually point homeowners toward the [Andersen 100 Series](/andersen), which meets the 2023 Oregon code's U-0.27 requirement and will not rot the way an old wood sill does. A single fogged unit in an otherwise sound ten-year-old window is not a reason to replace the whole house. We will say so plainly if that is all your home needs. ## The Short Version Fog on the inside means check your humidity. Fog on the outside on a cool morning means your windows are working. Fog that lives between the panes means a seal has failed, and it will not wipe off or fix itself. From there it is a question of how much of the window is compromised. Sometimes that is one pane of glass. Sometimes it is the whole opening. If you are not sure which one you are looking at, send us a photo or have us take a look. We will give you a straight answer and a free in-home quote in writing, and we will not try to sell you fifteen new windows to fix one. Call 541-639-3968 or [get a free quote](/contact).

faq.q: Can a foggy window be fixed without replacing the whole window?
faq.a: Often, yes. If the fog is on the inside surface, it is a humidity issue you can usually fix for free with ventilation. If the fog is trapped between the panes, the insulated glass unit's seal has failed, but if the frame and sash are still sound, a glass-only swap usually replaces the failed glass without touching the rest of the window.

faq.q: Is condensation on the outside of my windows in the morning a bad sign?
faq.a: No. Condensation on the outside of the glass on a cool, clear morning usually means your low-E glass is holding indoor heat in well enough that the outer pane runs colder than the dew point. Andersen Windows and other manufacturers describe this as a sign of energy efficiency, not a defect, and it clears on its own once the sun warms the glass.

faq.q: Why is there fog trapped between my window panes?
faq.a: Insulated glass units are sealed at the edge with a gas-filled gap between the panes. When that seal breaks down from age, sun, and years of water sitting against it, the gas escapes and moist air leaks in, condensing on the inner glass where it cannot be wiped away. The National Renewable Energy Laboratory has found that a failed seal can raise a window's U-factor by as much as 32%, so the window loses much of its insulating value, not only its clarity.

faq.q: What is the fix for fog between the panes?
faq.a: It depends on what else has failed. If the frame and sash are sound, a new sealed glass unit set into the existing sash is usually enough. If the frame is rotting, the sill is soft, or several windows are failing at once, a full-frame replacement is the better fix because it lets us repair the opening too. We look at the window in person and tell you which one makes sense.

faq.q: Why do window seals fail faster on some sides of the house?
faq.a: South- and west-facing glass takes the most direct sun and the biggest daily temperature swings, and Thompson Creek, a national window manufacturer, notes those windows commonly fail five to ten years earlier than north-facing ones on the same house. In Western Oregon, older windows also let winter rain sit against the bottom edge of the glass, which wears the seal out faster.

title: Why New Windows Pay Off in Roseburg & Eugene
excerpt: What wet winters and hot valley summers do to old windows in Roseburg and Eugene, what new ones fix, and how to read a window quote.
imageAlt: Black-framed replacement windows in a living room
body:
Roseburg and Eugene are good places to own a home and hard places to own an old window.

Both sit in climate zone 4C, the marine zone. That label sounds mild, and on paper it is. In practice it means months of gray, wet weather, rain that blows in sideways on a southwest wind, and then a dry summer when valley afternoons turn hot and west-facing glass soaks up sun until evening. A window here spends half the year keeping water out and the other half keeping heat out.

If your home was built before 2000, there is a good chance its windows were never made for either job. Here is what that does to your house.

## Windows Are a Quarter to a Third of Your Heating and Cooling

The U.S. Department of Energy attributes **25 to 30% of a home's heating and cooling energy use** to heat moving in and out through its windows. Not the walls. Not the roof. The windows.

That surprises people, because a window looks like a small part of a wall. But glass is a far worse insulator than the insulated framing around it, and a single-pane window is close to a bare sheet of glass between your living room and a cold, wet January night. In July the same glass works in reverse and lets the afternoon heat pour in.

Your furnace and your air conditioner do not know they are losing a race. They run longer.

## What Replacement Actually Does

This is where a lot of window companies start making numbers up, so we will keep it honest.

Be skeptical of anyone who promises to cut your energy bill in half. The research does not support it, and a contractor who will stretch a savings number will stretch other things too. Here is what new windows reliably do: hold temperature, stop drafts, quiet the room, and take away the cold edge you feel standing next to old glass in winter.

Replacing failing windows will lower your bills by a real amount. It will not make them disappear. The bigger change is how the house feels.

## Why People Here Actually Replace Their Windows

Nearly everyone we visit mentions the energy bill. Almost nobody is thinking only about the bill. What they describe is:

- **The cold room.** One room nobody uses from November to March because it never warms up. That is usually a window problem, not a furnace problem.
- **The hot room.** The west-facing bedroom that is still warm at bedtime in August. Low-E glass cuts a lot of that heat gain.
- **Wet sills and soft wood.** Rain that runs down the glass all winter collects at the sill. Old wood sills that stay wet start to rot, and failed flashing lets water into the wall below.
- **Fog between the panes.** Fog trapped between two panes means the seal has failed and the insulating gas is gone. That window now works like single-pane glass. It cannot be repaired, only replaced.
- **Smoke season.** When late-summer wildfire smoke settles into the valley, a window that seals tight keeps more of it outside. Old, loose sashes do not.
- **Noise.** Good double-pane glass noticeably cuts road noise. People with windows facing I-5 or a busy street bring this up as often as energy.
- **Windows that will not open.** Painted-shut, swollen, or broken-balance windows are a safety issue as much as a nuisance. Every bedroom needs a window that opens.

## What Our Climate Asks of a Replacement Window

Three things matter here more than people expect.

**U-factor.** This measures how much heat the whole window loses. Lower is better. The 2023 Oregon Residential Specialty Code calls for **U-0.27 or lower**. Any quote you get should state the U-factor in writing. If it does not, ask.

**A frame that shrugs off water.** In a wet climate the frame and sill matter as much as the glass. Materials that soak up water, swell, or need paint every few years are the ones that fail first here.

**Glass that handles summer sun.** A low-E coating keeps winter heat in and cuts summer heat gain on west and south walls. It also blocks most of the ultraviolet light that fades floors and furniture.

This is why we usually recommend the [Andersen 100 Series](/andersen) for homes around Roseburg and Eugene. Its Fibrex composite frame is rated at twice the strength of vinyl, it does not rot or need painting, the color runs through the material instead of sitting on top as paint, and it comes in ENERGY STAR certified configurations. When a project calls for a real wood interior, we step up to the 400 Series.

## About Rebates, the Honest Version

Two things have changed, and a lot of websites have not caught up.

First, **Energy Trust of Oregon ended its residential window incentives in Oregon at the start of 2026.** If you are a Pacific Power customer in Roseburg or anywhere else in Oregon, there is no Energy Trust window cash-back to count on.

Second, the **federal 25C tax credit for windows expired at the end of 2025.** If a contractor is still using a federal tax credit to close the sale, that is a reason to slow down.

The bright spot is Eugene. **EWEB runs its own window rebate** for customers with electric heat who are replacing single-pane or metal-frame windows. We walk through who qualifies in our [EWEB window rebate guide](/blog/eweb-window-rebate-eugene-oregon). When we quote, we check your situation and tell you straight if you do not qualify.

## What to Look for in Whoever Does the Work

A great window installed poorly will underperform an ordinary window installed well. In a climate this wet, the install is most of the outcome. When you compare quotes:

1. **Ask who is actually doing the work.** Not who is selling it. With us, Clancy is on every job.
2. **Ask for the CCB number and check it.** Oregon makes this easy to look up online. Ours is #260230.
3. **Ask for the U-factor in writing**, along with the product line and series.
4. **Ask how the opening gets flashed, sealed, and trimmed.** This is where installs quietly fail, and in Western Oregon it is where water gets in.
5. **Be wary of urgency.** A deal that only exists if you sign tonight is a sales tactic.

## The Short Version

Your windows account for a quarter to a third of your heating and cooling, and our long wet winters and hot valley summers are hard on old ones. Replacing failing single-pane windows lowers your bills by a real but limited amount, and it changes how the house feels a great deal more than that.

If you want to know what your home needs, we will come measure and tell you, including telling you if some of your windows are fine and can stay. That happens more often than you would think. Call 541-639-3968 or [get a free quote](/contact).

faq.q: What does replacing my windows actually do for my house?
faq.a: The U.S. Department of Energy attributes 25 to 30% of a home's heating and cooling energy use to heat moving in and out through its windows. New windows hold temperature, stop drafts, cut outside noise, and take away the cold edge you feel next to old glass in winter and the heat coming off it in summer. Be cautious of any contractor who leads with a dramatic savings percentage. The comfort difference is the part you live with every day.

faq.q: Is it worth replacing windows that are not broken?
faq.a: Sometimes yes, sometimes no, and we will tell you which. If your windows are single-pane, fogged between the panes, rotting at the sill, painted shut, or making rooms uncomfortable, replacement pays off in comfort and bills. If they are sound double-pane units in good shape, we will say so rather than sell you something you do not need.

faq.q: What U-factor should replacement windows have in Oregon?
faq.a: The 2023 Oregon Residential Specialty Code calls for a U-factor of 0.27 or lower. Some rebate programs ask for more: EWEB's standard window rebate in Eugene requires U-0.22 or lower. Any quote you receive should state the U-factor in writing. If it does not, ask before you sign.

faq.q: Can I get a rebate for replacing my windows in Roseburg or Eugene?
faq.a: It depends on your utility. Energy Trust of Oregon ended its Oregon window incentives at the start of 2026, and the federal 25C window tax credit expired at the end of 2025. In Eugene, EWEB offers its own window rebate for electric-heated homes replacing single-pane or metal-frame windows. We check your situation when we quote.

faq.q: How long does it take to replace the windows in a house?
faq.a: Once your windows arrive, a single opening usually takes one to three hours, and a full home of ten to fifteen windows is usually done in one to three days. The longer part of the timeline is manufacturing lead time, which we give you in writing with your quote.
